facebook.post: On this week's Longmont Locals episode, architect Steve Lane shared details about 600 Main, the community square project taking shape right across from the Pump House. The LDDA bought the old gas station site, remediated it, and gathered public input at Roosevelt Park on what people wanted to see there. Now it's turning into a downtown public park with a mobile stage for events, shipping-container visitor center and bathrooms, shade structures, and trees like hackberries and maples (which, as Steve notes, will take a while to grow). It's one of those projects that could really shift how we use downtown. What kind of events would you most want to see hosted there once it opens?

instagram.caption: Ever wonder why new buildings in Longmont take years to show up? On this week's Longmont Locals episode with Steve Lane of BAS1S Architecture, we break down the whole timeline: land contracts, entitlements, changing interest rates, and why developers can't just get the money first. Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: Why does every new building project in Longmont seem to take forever? This week on Longmont Locals, we sat down with Steve Lane of BAS1S Architecture and walked through the entire development timeline. Turns out you can't get financing until the city approves your plans, but you can't finalize plans without spending money on architects and engineers first. And by the time a project clears entitlements and secures funding, interest rates may have totally shifted. It's a multi-year process even for smaller projects, and now I finally understand why 'just build it already' isn't how any of this works. What's a project in Longmont you've been watching and waiting on?

bluesky.post: Why new buildings take years: you need city approval before you can get money, but you need money to pay for plans before you get approval. And rates change the whole time. Wild.

instagram.caption: Motion sensors that turn off your desk plug when you stop moving. Daylight sensors people immediately override. This week on Longmont Locals, architect Steve Lane of BAS1S walks us through the building code requirements that cost serious money but get defeated the moment someone plugs in a power strip. Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: We sat down with Steve Lane of BAS1S Architecture for this week's Longmont Locals episode, and he pulled back the curtain on some building code requirements that sound smart on paper but fall apart in practice. Case in point: occupancy sensors on outlets that shut off power when you're not moving enough, or daylight harvesting systems that dim the lights and get overridden five minutes later. The systems cost real money to install, save almost nothing in energy, and get defeated the moment someone brings in a power strip. It's the kind of insider perspective you only get from someone actually navigating these rules every day. What's a building code quirk or workaround you've run into in Longmont?

bluesky.post: Architect on building codes that waste money: outlets with occupancy sensors (defeated by a $12 power strip) and daylight harvesting systems that everyone immediately overrides. New clip from Longmont Locals.
